claims.text: Section 503 of the National Security Act of 1947. Subsection (c)(2) permits the President, on a determination that 'it is essential to limit access to the finding to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States,' to report a covert action finding only to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate -- the actual statutory Gang of Eight.

Subsection (c)(3) permits a finding not to be reported in advance at all in extraordinary circumstances, requiring only that the President thereafter report 'in a timely fashion' with 'a statement of the reasons for not giving prior notice.'

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) permits a covert action finding to be reported to 'the chairmen and ranking minority members of the congressional intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House of Representatives, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and such other member or members of the congressional leadership as may be included by the President.'

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(3) permits a finding not to be reported in advance at all, requiring only that the President thereafter 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with 'a statement of the reasons for not giving prior notice'.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that within 180 days of a statement of reasons for limited access the President ensure that all members of the intelligence committees get access, or submit a further statement of reasons.

50 U.S.C. 3093(d)(2) lists among the factors making an undertaking significant whether it 'requires an expansion of existing authorities, including authorities relating to research, development, or operations' and whether it 'results in the expenditure of significant funds or other resources'.
ICD 906 section C.3 records that the IC controlled access program regime does not apply to 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action'.

An activity characterised as covert action is reportable to no defense committee at all, and under 3093(c)(3) need not be reported to anyone in advance - making it the only regime weaker on prior notice than a waived DoD special access program. Reasoning: 3093 runs solely to the intelligence committees or the Gang of Eight, and (c)(3) removes even that.

desc: Section 503 of the National Security Act of 1947, added by the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1991, Public Law 102-88 of 14 August 1991, governs the one category of activity that sits outside every special access program reporting regime. ICD 906 section C.3 states in terms that neither it nor the DoD SAP regime applies to 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action'. Section 3093 requires a written presidential finding before any covert action, reported in writing to the intelligence committees 'as soon as possible after such approval and before the initiation of the covert action'. Subsection (c)(2) is the exception the press calls the Gang of Eight: where the President determines it essential to limit access 'to meet extraordinary circumstances affecting vital interests of the United States', the finding may go to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House, the majority and minority leaders of the Senate, and any other leadership members the President chooses to include. Subsection (c)(3) permits no prior notice at all, requiring only that the President afterwards 'fully inform the congressional intelligence committees in a timely fashion' with a statement of reasons. Subsection (c)(5), added in 2010, requires a written statement of reasons for limiting access and forces a reconsideration within 180 days - a protection with no counterpart in the SAP statutes. Subsection (d) extends the same notification rules to 'any significant change in a previously approved covert action' and lists the factors that make an undertaking significant, including whether it 'requires an expansion of existing authorities, including authorities relating to research, development, or operations' and whether it 'results in the expenditure of significant funds or other resources'. For this board the importance is structural: an activity characterised as covert action under NSC purview is reportable only under section 3093, is invisible to the defense committees entirely, and can lawfully be known to as few as eight members of Congress - or, under (c)(3), to none in advance.
